title: Non-finite and verbless clauses
description: Explore infinitival, gerund-participial, past-participial and verbless clauses, their subjects, complements, modifiers and catenative chains.
example: She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline.

key_terms.definition: A clause whose verb is infinitival or participial rather than a primary finite form.
A non-finite clause with a plain-form verb, either with to or bare.
An infinitival clause introduced by the subordinator to.
An infinitival clause with a plain-form verb and no to.
A non-finite clause headed by a gerund-participle in -ing.
A non-finite clause headed by a past participle.
A to-infinitival with an overt subject introduced by for.
A non-finite clause missing a non-subject element that is recovered from context.
A non-finite clause with no overt subject, interpreted from context.
A construction in which a verb takes a non-finite complement, often recursively.
A verb that licenses a catenative complement.
A non-finite complement that cannot be reduced to an object, predicative complement or PP complement.
A catenative construction with no intervening NP between the matrix and subordinate verbs.
A catenative construction with an intervening NP between the matrix and subordinate verbs.
A complex catenative construction with an intervening NP that is not introduced by a preposition.
A complex catenative construction in which for introduces the subject of the infinitival.
A complex catenative construction in which the intervening NP is the complement of a preposition.
A gerund-participial complement with a passive meaning, as in The house needs painting.
An intervening NP that is syntactically associated with the matrix verb but semantically associated with the subordinate verb.
A construction such as John is easy to please, with a hollow infinitival complement.
A non-finite or finite clause placed after dummy it in subject function.
A clause placed after dummy it in object function.
A complement ascribing a property to a predicand, which can be a non-finite clause.
An infinitival clause with interrogative type, as in whether to go.
An infinitival clause functioning as a relative modifier, as in a place to stay.
A clause with no verb, often functioning as an adjunct or supplement.
A verb phrase used before a noun that does not constitute a full non-finite clause.
The interpretation of an understood subject through another expression in the construction.

intro: Take *She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*. One sentence, several verbs, and only the first is finite. *Wanted* carries tense; *to arrange* and *to review* do not, and the subject of *review* is never spelled out. The rest of the sentence is built from clauses that have subjects, objects and complements but no primary tense.

This chapter starts with that finite/non-finite divide and with the three non-finite form-types. It then follows *to* and *for*, the auxiliaries that non-finites do and do not admit, subjectless and hollow clauses, and the catenative construction in its simple and complex shapes. Later sections turn to non-catenative complements, complements of adjectives, nouns and prepositions, modifiers, supplements and verbless clauses.

The catenative chain is the thread to hold on to. A catenative verb takes a non-finite complement, and the pattern can nest: *She intends to try to persuade him to help her redecorate*. Each verb heads a layer, and every intervening NP has to be attached to the right one.

blocks.text: Compare *She left* with *She wanted to leave*. The first has a verb with primary tense; the second has one too, but its complement does not. *I remember locking the door* and *He got charged* likewise contain clauses with verbs, subjects and objects but no primary tense. The plain form is the tricky case, because it appears on both sides of the line.

A plain form can be imperative (*Be patient*), subjunctive (*It is essential that he be careful*) or infinitival (*It is important for him to be careful*), yet only the last is non-finite. *To*, the absence of *do*-support, the embedding and the subject form separate the three.

Infinitivals normally carry *to*, except after modals and supportive *do*. Negation goes before *to*, not through *do*: *It’s important not to be late*, never *to don’t be late*. They are typically embedded, and when a subject appears it is accusative or plain, often behind *for*.

blocks.text: The verb form sorts non-finite clauses into three types. *Max wanted to change his name* is infinitival; *I remember locking the door* is gerund-participial; *His father got charged with manslaughter* is past-participial. The label comes from the verb, not from the function the clause performs.

Infinitivals split again. *They forced me to sign* has *to*; *They helped me move the furniture* does not. The to-infinitival appears across a wide range of constructions, while the bare form is largely confined to complements of a small verb class, modals and supportive *do* included.

The old gerund/present participle split does not survive inspection. The gerund-participle is one verb form, whether it appears in a progressive construction or heads a non-finite clause. Two labels for one form hide the syntax they share.

blocks.text: *To* is the default marker of the infinitival, and *for* is what lets it have an overt subject: *For them to take the children could endanger the mission*. *For* cannot appear without a subject, and that subject is accusative or plain — *for him to go*, not *for he to go*.

Bare infinitivals drop *to*. They follow modals (*can go*), supportive *do* (*did go*), and lexical verbs such as *help*, *make*, *let* and *see*: *They made him apologise*, *We saw her leave*. A few idiomatic constructions use the bare form too.

Whether *to* appears is not free variation. Some verbs take only to-infinitivals, some only bare ones, and some take both with a meaning difference. *I helped him move* and *I helped him to move* are near synonyms; *I made him move* and *I made him to move* are not.

blocks.text: Modals and supportive *do* are shut out of non-finite clauses. The other auxiliaries are not. *I expect to have finished*, *I expect to be working* and *I expect to be interviewed* show perfect *have*, progressive *be* and passive *be* inside an infinitival.

Gerund-participials admit perfect *have* and passive *be* — *I regret having told them*, *I resent being given so little notice* — but not productive progressive *be*. *I remember being working* is not an established construction; the progressive meaning is carried by the simple *-ing* form itself.

Past participles do two jobs in non-finite clauses. The perfect participle follows auxiliary *have* and can stack with progressive or passive *be*: *has seen*, *has been seeing*, *has been seen*. The passive participle heads a clause that takes no auxiliaries at all: *He had it checked by the manager*.

blocks.text: Most non-finite clauses say nothing about their subject. *Kim was glad to reach home*, *It has been a pleasure meeting you*, *Anyone living nearby will be evacuated* and *The sum spent on gambling was extraordinary* all leave the subject to context. That absence is normal, not a defect.

*Kim was glad to reach home* and *Anyone living nearby will be evacuated* both contain clauses without an overt subject. They are still clauses: a VP heads each one, and the missing subject is supplied by interpretation. The exception is the attributive VP inside an NP — *our rapidly approaching deadline*, *a poorly drafted report* — which allows far less structure.

*The letter isn’t legible enough for you to read* is missing the object of *read*, understood as *the letter*. *I don’t think they are worth spending much time on* is missing the complement of *on*, understood as *they*. Hollow clauses lack an internal element rather than a subject.

blocks.text: Watch what happens when one verb takes another as its complement: *I wanted to arrange for Kim to do it*, *She intends to try to persuade him to help her redecorate*. The verbs stack, each heading its own layer, and the stack can keep growing. That stacking is the catenative construction.

In the simple pattern no NP comes between the verbs. *I hope to finish soon*, *I helped wash up*, *I stopped worrying about it* and *I got arrested* all attach the non-finite complement directly to the matrix verb.

*She wants a holiday* and *She wants to leave* look like the same verb with different fillers, but the second complement is a clause, not an object. The test is the verb’s range: *want* takes both, and neither reduces to the other. That is the catenative relation.

blocks.text: Add an NP between the verbs and the construction becomes complex. *I advised you to sell it* and *I made them apologise* both have an intervening NP, and that NP may lean semantically towards the matrix verb or towards the subordinate one. Which way it leans changes the reading.

The plain-complex pattern leaves the NP bare: *I persuaded Liz to go*, *I intended Liz to go*. The for-complex pattern introduces it with *for*: *I arranged for her to go by bus*. The oblique-complex pattern makes it the complement of a preposition: *I signalled to her to move off the road*.

Gerund-participial complexes show the same tension. *I caught him doing it* and *I resented him doing it* differ in where *him* belongs semantically, and *I saw him doing it* adds the perception verb’s own interpretive pattern. The surface shape is identical; the argument structure is not.

blocks.text: Why not call the non-finite complement an object? Because the same verb takes ordinary objects elsewhere without the two behaving alike. *She wants a holiday* has an object; *She wants to leave* has a clause. The clause has its own auxiliaries and its own internal structure, none of which an NP object brings.

Auxiliaries fit the same analysis. In *She may like it*, *may* takes the non-finite complement *like it*, which makes it a catenative verb. Treating auxiliaries this way — the catenative-auxiliary analysis — explains the layering in *may have been seen*, where each auxiliary heads its own layer.

The traditional gerund/participle distinction plays no role here. *Gerund-participle* names the form; *gerund-participial* names the clause type. The same form appears in progressive constructions and in non-finite complements, and one description covers both more economically than two.

blocks.text: Catenative verbs sort into three classes by where they occur. Class 1 is simple only: *hope*, *seem*, *stop*, *get*. Class 2 is both: *want*, *help*, *see*. Class 3 is complex only: *persuade*, *advise*, *arrange*.

*Hope* occurs only in the simple construction, *persuade* only in the complex one, and *want* in both. These are complement patterns, not semantic essences. A verb can shift class with its sense, and the classification describes what it licenses, not what kind of verb it is.

Form-type cuts across the classes. Some verbs take to-infinitivals, some gerund-participials, some bare infinitivals, and some take more than one with a difference. *Remember locking* looks back; *remember to lock* looks forward. *Stop smoking* and *stop to smoke* differ in how the complement relates to the matrix event.

blocks.text: The gap in *John is easy to please* is easy to miss. Nothing is missing from the subject position; what is missing is the object of *please*, and the sentence supplies John. Compare *They are worth spending time on*, where the complement of *on* is the gap and the matrix subject fills it. The gap is internal; the subject is not what is missing.

*John is easy to please* has no overt object of *please*; *The letter isn’t legible enough to read* has no overt object of *read*. A subjectless clause has no overt subject, while a hollow clause has no overt object or other internal dependent. The missing element can be an object, a prepositional complement or another internal dependent.

The pattern clusters around adjectives such as *easy*, *difficult*, *ready* and *worth*, and around *enough* and *too*. What fills the gap depends on the matrix subject or object, and the relation is not always a simple copy of an NP.

blocks.text: *Kim wants to go* and *Kim persuaded Pat to go* both leave the goer unspoken, but they point to different people: Kim in the first, Pat in the second. *Kim seems to like them* adds a third relation, where Kim is the subject of *seems* and the liker at once.

When another expression supplies that subject, the relation is control. *Want* is a subject-control verb: the matrix subject controls. *Persuade* is object-control: the matrix object controls. *Promise* is subject control despite a prominent object — *Kim promised Pat to go* means Kim goes.

*Kim seems to like them* and *Kim wants to like them* look alike, but Kim has a different relation to each verb. In the first, Kim is the subject of *seems* and is not a semantic argument of *seem*; the paraphrase *It seems that Kim likes them* shows the split. In the second, Kim supplies the subject of *like*. Surface similarity hides the difference between sharing a subject and supplying one.

Some subjectless clauses take a generic subject instead: *To err is human*, *It is important to be careful*. Nobody in the matrix supplies the missing subject; people in general do. Context and the matrix predicate decide whether the subject is controlled, raised, arbitrary or recovered from discourse.

options.text: Control supplies the understood subject from a matrix NP; raising associates a matrix NP semantically with the subordinate verb.
options.feedback: Both leave the non-finite subject unexpressed, but the relations differ.

options.text: Control clauses are finite; raising clauses are non-finite.

blocks.text: *To underestimate her would be foolish* shows an infinitival in subject position, and *I call that taking liberties* shows a gerund-participial clause as a predicative complement. Objects are open too: *I found talking to her quite helpful*. Non-finite clauses take the ordinary clause functions, not only the catenative one.

They extrapose as well. *It was natural to be worried* has an extraposed subject, and *I found it distressing to see her so ill* has an extraposed object. Dummy *it* holds the core position while the clause sits after the predicate.
So the catenative/non-catenative line is functional, not formal. The same clause can be a catenative complement with one verb and a subject or object with another. The matrix construction decides.

sections.title: Complements of adjectives, nouns, and prepositions

blocks.text: Non-finite complements attach to more than verbs. Adjectives take them (*keen to regain control*), nouns take them (*the opportunity to have my say*), and prepositions take them (*in order to catch the train*). Some are licensed by the adjacent word, others indirectly by the larger matrix.

Interrogative and relative infinitivals extend the range: *I can’t decide whether to go*, *He doesn’t know how to placate her*, *funds with which to conduct a survey*, *a place to stay*. Non-finite syntax here meets interrogative or relative syntax.

Function depends on the governing construction, not on meaning alone. *She left at six to catch the train* has a purpose modifier in clause structure; *in order to catch the train* has a complement inside a PP. Both express purpose; they do not occupy the same slot.

blocks.text: *I’ve found a box to keep the tapes in* embeds an infinitival inside the NP; *She left at six to catch the early train* attaches one to the clause. Both modify rather than complement. Non-finite clauses can hang from a nominal or from a whole clause, and the two relations are not interchangeable.
*He’s a charlatan, to put it bluntly* adds a supplement. It comments on the clause or on the act of speaking rather than filling a slot, and it is prosodically detached — usually set off by a comma.

*She left at six to catch the early train* and *He’s a charlatan, to put it bluntly* both use a non-finite clause, but one modifies the event and the other comments on the act of speaking. The range of meanings is wider than finite content clauses allow in the same positions: purpose, result, condition, concession or comment. Syntax identifies the relation; semantics has to say which one.

blocks.text: Some clauses have no verb at all: *With the windows open, the room stayed cool*, *Although tired, she kept working*, *The meeting over, everyone left*. The missing verb is understood, and the construction still has internal structure and a relation to the matrix.

*With the windows open* describes a circumstance; *The meeting over* gives a temporal relation. Neither contains a verb, which is why verbless clauses are not a fourth non-finite type: the three non-finite types are defined by verb form. A verbless clause usually contains a subject and a predicative complement or a PP.
*With the windows open* and *The meeting over* show how common the pattern is with *with* and *without* and in supplement-like absolutes.

blocks.text: *To leave*, *having left* and *left* show the three non-finite verb forms in action: infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial. *For* and *to* mark subjects and infinitival status, and modals and supportive *do* are excluded from the non-finite system.

Non-finite clauses can be subjectless, hollow or catenative. Hollow clauses lack a non-subject element recovered from context; catenative constructions chain verbs through non-finite complements, either directly or across an intervening NP.

Beyond catenative use, non-finite clauses serve as subjects, objects, predicative complements, complements of adjectives, nouns and prepositions, modifiers and supplements. Verbless clauses form a separate construction, identified by the absence of a verb rather than by a verb inflection.

blocks.title: A non-finite checklist
blocks.text: Identify the verb form and the clause boundaries. Decide whether the clause is infinitival, gerund-participial or past-participial. Check for for and to, an overt or understood subject, and any missing non-subject element. Then identify its function in the matrix.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes hollow from subjectless clauses?

options.text: A hollow clause lacks a non-subject element; a subjectless clause lacks an overt subject.
A hollow clause has no verb.
A subjectless clause is always finite.

worked: Take *She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*. The matrix clause is *She wanted ...*; its catenative complement is *to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*. The verb *arrange* then takes the for-complex complement *for the committee to review the proposal*.

Inside that complement, *for* introduces the subject *the committee* of the to-infinitival *to review the proposal*. The example contains a catenative chain of three verbs, a for-complex construction, and a subjectless infinitival inside the for-clause. Each layer has its own head and complement structure.
application: Find each verb and the non-finite clause it licenses. Identify the form-type: to-infinitival, bare infinitival, gerund-participial or past-participial. Check whether there is an overt subject, a for phrase, or an intervening NP.

Decide whether the construction is simple or complex catenative. In a simple construction the non-finite complement follows the matrix verb directly. In a complex construction an NP intervenes and may belong with either verb.

Then identify the clause’s function in the larger structure: catenative complement, subject, object, predicative complement, adjective/noun/PP complement, modifier or supplement. Check for hollow elements and for verbless clauses, which lack a verb altogether.
reveal: In *She wanted to arrange for the committee to review the proposal before the deadline*, *wanted* takes the to-infinitival complement *to arrange ...*. *Arrange* takes the for-complex complement *for the committee to review the proposal*. *For* introduces the subject of the infinitival, and *review* takes *the proposal* as object.
recap: Non-finite clauses have three main form-types: infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial. Infinitivals can be to or bare, and for introduces an overt subject. Modal auxiliaries and supportive do are excluded from non-finite clauses.

Catenative constructions chain verbs through non-finite complements. Hollow clauses lack a non-subject element, subjectless clauses lack an overt subject, and verbless clauses lack a verb. Non-finite clauses also function as ordinary subjects, objects, complements, modifiers and supplements.
